This theme of abandonment echoes v. 29. The aggregation of curses here is overwhelming. This chapter should be compared with the similar but shorter Lev. 26, which ends with the possibility of confession, repentance, and restoration. Here, the theme of possible restoration is left for ch. 30.

verse_quote: the covenant ... in the land of Moab.
note:
Scholars debate whether v. 1 concludes what precedes or introduces what follows. The latter, as reflected in the ESV text division, is more likely. This “covenant ... in the land of Moab” is a renewal of the Sinai covenant (“the covenant ... at Horeb”). As usual, Moses recites the history of God’s mighty acts on Israel’s behalf in the exodus from Egypt and in the wilderness (cf. Moses’s speech in 1:6–4:38). There follows a warning against departing from the Lord, a promise of restoration upon repentance, and a solemn charge to obey.

**Horeb.** See note on 1:6.
The deliverance from Egypt, which occupies a third of the book of Exodus, is mentioned many times in Deuteronomy (e.g., 1:30; 4:20, 34; 5:6; 11:2–7).
LORD **has not given ... eyes to see.** Paul combines this verse with Is. 29:10 and applies both verses to the Jews of his day (Rom. 11:8).

The special preservation of clothes is mentioned in 8:4. The additional fact given here is that they have drunk no wine or other fermented drink, since there are no grapes in the desert. They have also had no bread, but God has supplied them with manna.

In terming this a renewal of the Sinai covenant, we should remember that the covenant is the same, but the people are not. All those over twenty years of age at Sinai have perished in the wilderness. Many of the people under twenty years of age at that point are now between the ages of forty and sixty, and they saw the great events at Sinai. Now they, too, are to affirm their personal commitment to God by renewing the covenant.

verse_quote: the sweeping away of moist and dry alike.
note: The Hebrew of this phrase (apparently an ancient proverb) is difficult to translate. The entire phrase as translated here means that the sinner will not escape judgment by hiding undetected in the company of the righteous (cf. v. 21). Another possibility is to render the phrase “so that the well-watered land is destroyed along with dry land” or “so that the drunkard is destroyed along with the thirsty,” indicating that the sin of one brings disaster on many (cf. vv. 22–25). Another possible translation is “to add drunkenness to thirst,” meaning that the sinful man compounds his guilt by sinking further into sin.
See note on 28:61 (cf. Josh. 1:7, 8).

The four cities of the plain that were destroyed in Abraham’s day are named. In Gen. 14 five cities of the plain are mentioned but not their destruction. In Gen. 19 Sodom and Gomorrah are mentioned, and the whole area is said to be destroyed, but Zoar is spared. Deuteronomy puts the two records together and lists the four destroyed cities. The judgment of Sodom is a prophetic model of divine wrath. Like Moses, Isaiah compares the judgment of Israel to that of Sodom (Is. 1:10). Jesus also compares the judgment at His second coming to that of Sodom (Luke 17:28–35), as does Peter (2 Pet. 2:6).

The meaning of the latter part of this verse is apparent: God’s revealed instruction is of vital importance, and the Israelites and their children must follow this teaching. The reference to “secret things” may suggest that Moses anticipates the uncertain future of the nation, remembering their waywardness and how they turned to the golden calf at Horeb (Ex. 32). In this uncertainty, Moses trusts the hidden future to his trustworthy God.

Anticipating the real possibility of judgment and exile for Israel, Moses looks beyond the time of judgment to Israel’s future repentance, restoration, and divine blessing. Significantly, this future blessing will include deliverance from slavery to sin. Moses’s reference to the circumcision of the “heart” (v. 6; cf. 10:16) is foundational for the later prophetic expectation (Jer. 31:31–34; Ezek. 36:25–27), and it finds fulfillment in the NT (Rom. 2:29).

verse_quote: with all your heart and with all your soul.
note: Moses refers again to the great commandment of 6:5, holding out the hope of repentance even when there has been apostasy and judgment.
The measure of God’s compassion in restoration will exceed the measure of His wrath in judgment and exile., 5

LORD **... will circumcise your heart.** See notes on vv. 1–10 and 10:16. The promised restoration and renewal will result from a sovereign work of God in the hearts of His elect. By circumcising (transforming) their hearts, He will replace their total inability and stubbornness (5:29; 10:16; 29:4) with the humility and repentance they need (cf. vv. 1, 2), purifying for Himself a people who will love and obey Him. See “Legalism” at Matt. 23:4.

The future restoration will bring a fulfillment of the promise made to Abraham and his seed: “Him who dishonors you I will curse” (Gen. 12:3). Moses links the restoration pictured in vv. 3–10 to a future judgment by God against the enemies of His people.

The blessings of the renewed covenant will be inseparable from, but not based on, the obedience of the restored remnant of the people to their Lord’s commandments (cf., e.g., Matt. 7:21). The obedience of Christ, which is the victory over sin in which the remnant by faith will share, is the only meritorious basis of such blessings (1 Cor. 1:30–31; 2 Cor. 5:21; Eph. 2:8–10).

Recalling his words in 6:6, Moses maintains that the covenant obligations God revealed through him and the righteousness required are readily accessible to and attainable by Israel (v. 11)—if they will seek such things properly, namely, by trusting only in the Lord and His mercy. He anticipates, however, that those with uncircumcised hearts and ears will raise questions denying these truths and will seek to establish a righteousness of their own (vv. 12, 13). Moses rebukes such stubbornness, insisting that the word of righteousness is found “in your mouth and in your heart” (v. 14)—in the mouth and heart that speak not in the unbelief and rebellion of their own imperfect righteousness but in the faith and humility of the Lord’s perfect righteousness alone. This righteousness the Lord has demonstrated to Israel in the works of salvation and judgment by which He confirmed His oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (cf. 8:17, 18; 9:4–6; 30:1–7; esp. 1:29–33; 9:23). The commandment that Moses proclaims here is a word calling for trust in God and His promises alone, and the righteousness it reveals is a righteousness attained only by faith (cf. v. 10 note; Gen. 15:6 note).

Paul later alludes to these verses in Rom. 10:6–8, updating Moses’s admonition in view of the revelation of God’s righteousness in the person and work of Christ. Paul preaches the word that calls for faith where Moses had to leave off, insisting that Israel (and the Gentiles) must now confess with their mouths that Jesus is Lord (Rom. 10:12, 13; cf. Deut. 6:4), and believe with their hearts that God raised Him from the dead (Rom. 10:9). God’s work in Jesus Christ yet again reveals His righteousness (Rom. 3:21–26) and confirms His oath to the fathers (cf. Rom. 4:18–25; Gal. 3). See “Special Revelation and the Bible” at Ex. 32:16.

Moses calls for a decision. There are two ways: life or death, God’s blessing or sure judgment. Joshua later presents the same alternatives (Josh. 24:15), and Jesus, who is greater than Moses or Joshua, calls His disciples to take the narrow path that leads to life (Matt. 7:13, 14).

The mention of witnesses recalls the form of ancient Near Eastern treaty documents, which have a list of witnesses at the end, often the names of pagan gods. In the biblical covenant, God’s creation is called to witness against His people because He alone is the Lord and there are no gods beside Him.

In this final section of his work, Moses provides for a smooth transition in covenant administration after his death. Also included are the Song of Moses and Moses’s blessing of the twelve tribes. The book concludes with an obituary for Moses.

**31:1 Moses continued to speak.** This brief exhortation (vv. 1–8) can hardly be called another address but is part of Moses’s arrangement of his final affairs and the transfer of authority to his successor Joshua (Introduction: Outline).

Acts 7:30 tells us that Moses spent forty years in Midian tending sheep. This time was not wasted, as he learned the geography and climate of the Sinai Peninsula in preparation for leading the Israelites in that area for another forty years. The humiliation of being reduced from a prince in Egypt to a hired tender of sheep also accomplished the divine disciplinary purpose of preparing Moses for his greater role as shepherd of God’s people. This leaves forty years for Moses’s youth and training in Egypt. Thus, God ensured that Moses was well prepared for his great task.

**no longer able to go out and come in.** Moses anticipates that he will soon die and no longer participate in the regular affairs of the community. Moses’s many-faceted role as Israel’s leader is coming to an end.

See notes on 1:37 and 3:23-28. Though the aged Moses is still active (34:7), the conquest of Canaan will require some years, and it is time for the younger man to take charge. Most importantly, the Lord Himself will lead Israel under Joshua as He has done with Moses (Ex. 33:14, 15).
These and the following words resemble the encouragement God gives Joshua after Moses died (Josh. 1:9).
The transfer of leadership is often a delicate matter. Moses wisely, and at God’s command, elevates Joshua in the presence of the people.

The conclusion of Moses’s covenant ministry is marked by the recording in writing of Moses’s speech (vv. 24–26; 28:61 note). Repeatedly in Exodus and in Deuteronomy, Moses is said to have written down the regulations and instructions given by the Lord. In Leviticus most of the chapters begin with the words, “The Lord spoke to Moses.” God used Moses preeminently to speak and write His word for Israel.

Moses provides for regular instruction of the people and their children in the covenant stipulations by the priests at a point in the year when the people have ample time to learn. The Feast of Booths comes in the fall and lasts a week (16:13–17 note). During the sabbatical year the land is to lie fallow, and the people will not be burdened with agricultural duties (15:1 note). This practice of reading the covenant stipulations at regular intervals was characteristic of the suzerainty treaties among nations of Moses’s time, which typically provided for the regular publication of the covenantal terms of agreement (see Introduction: Date and Occasion).

Joshua’s legitimacy and authority as Moses’s successor are underscored by his commission at the tent of meeting (that is, the tabernacle), accompanied by God’s appearance in the pillar of cloud (cf. Num. 12:4–12).

Knowing the people’s inclination to be unfaithful (v. 21), and realizing the power of song in worship and in memory, the Lord commands Moses to write a song that will serve as a testimony in future days. Other examples of poetry associated with Moses include Ex. 15:1–18; 32:18; Num. 10:35, 36; and Ps. 90.
Moses called heaven and earth as witnesses at the end of the covenant renewal in 30:19.
LORD **.** This song is to witness in future days to the Lord, His goodness, and His saving work for Israel (31:19).

This chapter provides the first instances in Scripture of “Rock” as a name for God (vv. 15, 18, 30; there is a similar image in Gen. 49:24 using a different Hebrew word). Suggesting God’s steadfast faithfulness and permanence, the term is common in the Psalms and other poetic passages (Ps. 95:1; Is. 44:8).
Note the sharp contrast between the steadfast, righteous God (v. 4) and the corrupt nation (v. 5).

The meaning here is that God by decree gave the Promised Land to Israel. It was an ancient grant to the patriarchs (v. 7).

**according to ... the sons of God.** Moses is recalling the ancient days (Gen. 10, the table of nations and the dividing of peoples) in order to make the point that Israel alone is selected in the midst of the dispersion of tribes and nations for the Lord’s special vocation. God is sovereign over all of history, but history itself is ordered in the interests of God’s plan of redemption for His chosen people Israel (Gen. 12:3).

verse_quote: as the apple of his eye.
note: A reference to the pupil of the eye. Just as the pupil of the eye is closely guarded against harm, so God protects Israel. God’s people are thus at the very core and heart of God’s vision.
The image is of an eagle teaching its young to fly. The poetic figures of the Song of Moses are powerful expressions of God’s dealings with His people. See also Gen. 1:2 and note.
See note at 3:1.

From the Hebrew term for “upright” _(yashar)._ Often used to represent Israel as the upright people of a holy and righteous God (33:5, 26; Is. 44:2), here the term is used ironically.

**grew fat, and kicked.** Israel is described with the telling figure of a well-fed ox.
See theological note “Demons.”

Just as Israel provoked God by worshiping that which was “no god,” so God will provoke them by means of “those who are no people” (people outside the sphere of the Mosaic covenant). This prophecy is partly fulfilled in the OT as Israel is defeated by God’s instruments of judgment, the Assyrians and Babylonians (Is. 10:5; Jer. 21:4–10). In the NT, Paul finds further fulfillment of this verse in the extension of the gospel to the Gentiles (Rom. 10:19; 11:11).

verse_quote: a fire is kindled ... to the depths of Sheol.
note: For the figure of God’s anger as a consuming fire, see Ps. 21:9; Jer. 15:14; 17:4. The poetic figure here represents God’s wrath as an all-devouring fire that burns to the deepest grave, consumes the surface of the earth, and reaches to the roots of the mountains. “Sheol” is often simply a term for the grave, but it may also refer to the location where the wicked go after death to await final judgment.

Though Israel deserves utter destruction because of her disobedience (v. 26), the Lord preserves a remnant of the people, lest the Gentiles take credit for their victory over Israel and fail to see God’s hand in history. Assyria and Babylon are later judged for their arrogant misunderstanding (Is. 10:12–19; 47:6–8).

Numbers are of no consequence when the Lord intervenes. Israel with God’s help will put to flight vast numbers of adversaries (Lev. 26:8), while a numerous but disobedient Israel will be defeated by a few, even fleeing when no one pursues (Lev. 26:17).
False gods bring evil deeds and poisonous fruit. Sodom symbolizes awful destruction (29:23 note).
The NT quotes this verse twice, using a slightly different wording (Rom. 12:19; Heb. 10:30).
Israel must see that they have no help apart from the one true God.

The Hebrew emphasizes by repetition. This whole stanza is a towering expression of the uniqueness of God in His being, power, providence, and justice. Because God is both infinitely just and all-powerful, we can be sure that evil will at last be destroyed (Rev. 19:1, 2).

The Septuagint and one of the Dead Sea Scrolls contain a longer version of this phrase (text note). This longer version is possibly quoted in Heb. 1:6.

**he avenges the blood of his children.** This triumphal Song of Moses is echoed at the consummation of human history (Rev. 19:2).

Moses emphasizes again that obedience to God’s commands, from the heart, is a matter of life—eternal life—and death (30:19, 20). Because sinners cannot render the perfect obedience that the Lord commands, the obedience that secures eternal life is ultimately the obedience of another—Jesus Christ, the perfect Lamb of God prefigured in the OT sacrifices (Rom. 3:21–26; 5:12–21; Heb. 9:1–10:18).

Usually identified as the modern Jebel Neba, a mountain twelve miles (19 km) east of the Jordan River’s point of entry into the Dead Sea. Rising over four thousand feet (1,219 m) above the Dead Sea, Mount Nebo will provide Moses a vantage point from which to view the Promised Land.

In Gen. 49, Leah’s children are listed first, followed by those of the handmaidens and Rachel. Here the order is different. Reuben, the firstborn, is mentioned first (v. 6), followed by the royal tribe of Judah (v. 7; cf. Gen. 49:10) and the priestly tribe of Levi (vv. 8–11). The tribes descending from Rachel’s sons are next (vv. 12–17), followed by two remaining sons of Leah, Zebulun and Issachar (vv. 18, 19). Finally, the servants’ children are listed (vv. 20–24). The tribe of Simeon is omitted, perhaps to retain the number twelve, although Jacob’s blessing predicted that Simeon would be scattered throughout Israel (Gen. 49:7).

**33:1 the man of God.** This expression is used customarily for prophets (1 Sam. 9:6; 1 Kin. 13:1; 17:18; 2 Kin. 4:7) but is applied to Moses only here and in the title of Ps. 90.

LORD **came from Sinai.** The defining event of Moses’s ministry, the revelation at Sinai, is recalled in terms describing the theophany on the mountain (Ex. 19:18; cf. Hab. 3:3).

**holy ones.** This is likely a reference to the angels of the heavenly host surrounding God’s throne (cf. 1 Kin. 22:19; Dan. 7:9, 10). The NT also mentions the role of angels in giving the Mosaic law (Acts 7:53; Gal. 3:19; Heb. 2:2 and note).
A reference to the Lord as king over His people (cf. 1 Sam. 12:12; Ps. 10:16). Moses is never called a king. On “Jeshurun,” see note 32:15.
This reading could reflect the curse on Reuben in Gen. 49:3, 4.

This blessing hints at the warrior role of the Davidic kings, descendants of Judah, in leading Israel into battle. But the blessing on Judah is extremely brief in view of the promise of rulership to Judah in Gen. 49:8–12 and in view of Judah’s large part in later history. Because a later writer might have wanted to give Judah more prominence, the brevity of this blessing points to a date of composition during Moses’s lifetime.

The blessing on Levi reflects the tribe’s fidelity at the time of the golden calf, when the Levites rallied to Moses’s side and acted in judgment against their sinful brethren (Ex. 32:27–29).

**Thummim ... Urim.** See note on Ex. 28:30.

Moses alludes to Ex. 3:4.

**prince among his brothers.** The Hebrew word translated “prince among” is sometimes used for one who is set apart by the Nazirite vow (cf. Num. 6:1–21 note). See Gen. 49:26. This may be the basis for Jesus being called a Nazarene in Matt. 2:23.

During this period, Ephraim is smaller than Manasseh (Num. 26:34, 37), but Ephraim will become more numerous and important (cf. Gen. 48:17–20). Because of the tribe’s importance, the name “Ephraim” is later applied to the ten tribes making up the northern kingdom of Israel (2 Chr. 25:7; Hos. 5:3, 11–14).

See note on 3:1. This blessing may refer to the northern settlement of Dan, located near Bashan (Judg. 18:27–29). More likely, a comparison of Dan to the strength and ferocity of the lions inhabiting the forests of Bashan may be in view.
Olive oil, valuable for food and also as fuel for lamps, is here symbolic of the tribe’s material prosperity (Gen. 49:20; cf. Job 29:6).

This final stanza has blessed the hearts of God’s people through the ages. He is the majestic God (v. 26), the eternal God (v. 27), the protecting and providing God (v. 28). The great blessing of Israel was that He was their God. The great blessing of the new covenant church is that this same God is our God. Such a splendid hymn of praise is perhaps only matched by passages in the NT such as “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” in Rev. 15:3, 4.

**33:26 Jeshurun.** See 32:15 and note.

This chapter is a supplement. Many suggest that it was added by the author of the book of Joshua in order to connect his work with the books of Moses, though it also could have been the addition of a later editor (Introduction: Author).

**34:1 Gilead as far as Dan.** The descriptions here and in v. 2 name the areas in terms of the tribal areas as designated in the book of Joshua (Josh. 13–19).
See note on 31:2.

The same period of mourning as for Aaron (Num. 20:29; cf. Gen. 50:3, 10; 2 Sam. 1:12). Ritual displays of mourning in the OT include weeping, fasting, tearing of clothing, wearing sackcloth, and throwing dust on the head (Gen. 37:34, 35; Ps. 35:13; Lam. 2:10). Certain mourning practices were forbidden to Israel (14:1 note).

verse_quote: spirit of wisdom ... laid his hands on him.
note: Moses previously put his hand on Joshua to symbolize the transfer of divinely ordained leadership (Num. 27:18). God empowers those whom He chooses and ordains for service.

**34:10 since.** Because no length of time is specified, these words need not imply that many generations had passed since Moses’s death. Joshua took Moses’s place, but he realized that Moses’s miracles and access to God had been unique (Num. 12:6–8).

The miraculous displays of God’s power in Egypt at the time of the exodus. Jesus arose as a prophet like Moses yet superior to him. He did miracles, signs, and wonders before the kings and rulers of the people and in the sight of all Israel (Matt. 4:23–25; John 20:30–31; Acts 2:22; 3:22–26).
